review_flags: The text says 'There are only 91 possible labels for objects, chosen by the COCO dataset creators', derived from `max(max(x["labels"]) ...) + 1`. That expression gives the size of the integer ID range (0..90), not the number of object classes: COCO 2017 detection annotations use 80 categories with non-contiguous IDs between 1 and 90 (several IDs are unused and 0 is not a category). 91 is the right size for a classification output indexed by raw ID, but it is not the number of distinct labels.
generation.extraction_quality: Clean extraction. Element p358_e06 merges two printed paragraphs ('We can use a KerasHub utility…' and 'Let's visualize an example image…'); they are annotated separately. Listing 12.4 is cut at the page break inside `draw_box`; the rest (label text box and `draw_image`) is on p.359. The callout 'Uses the golden ratio to generate new hues of a bright color with the HSV colorspace' was split into three fragments and re-read from the image.

overview.title: Inspecting COCO and drawing labelled boxes
overview.section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch
overview.main_topic: Dataset statistics of the parsed COCO metadata, mapping label IDs to names with KerasHub, and the first half of the Matplotlib box-drawing utilities
overview.central_idea: The parsed training set has 117,266 annotated images with 1 to 63 boxes each and integer labels up to 90. Labels are turned into names with `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name`, and listing 12.4 starts the drawing helpers: a per-label colour generator that steps the hue by the golden ratio, and a `draw_box` function based on Matplotlib rectangles.
overview.importance: Inspecting data before modelling is a habit the book insists on. The helpers defined here are reused throughout the chapter to show ground truth, YOLO targets and model predictions (pp.359–373).
learning_objectives: Read the output of listing 12.3 and state the dataset's size, box-count range and label range
Interpret one record (`metadata[435]`): normalized boxes, label IDs and file path
Explain the golden-ratio hue trick in `label_to_color` and compute the first few hues
Explain how `draw_box` uses a Matplotlib `Rectangle` patch with normalized coordinates

paragraphs.excerpt: We have 117,266 images. Each image can have anywhere from 1 to 63
paragraphs.what_it_says: There are 117,266 images, each with 1 to 63 boxed objects, and only 91 possible labels, chosen by the COCO creators.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Detection targets are variable-length: one image may contain a single object, another 63. Any model or target encoding must handle this — YOLO does so with a fixed grid (p.360).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The label count fixes the size of the class output; the box-count range shows why the outputs cannot be a fixed list of boxes per image.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): 117,266 is the number of train2017 images with at least one annotation (COCO train2017 has about 118k images; those without annotations never enter `metadata`, p.357). The '91' is max ID + 1; COCO 2017 uses 80 category IDs scattered in 1..90.

terminology.meaning: Integer COCO category ID attached to each box.

connections: p.357: `metadata` is built from the annotations loop
p.360: YOLO handles variable object counts with a grid and per-cell confidence

paragraphs.excerpt: We can use a KerasHub utility `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name(id)` to map these
paragraphs.what_it_says: `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name(id)` maps integer labels to human-readable names, similar to the ImageNet decoding utility used in chapter 8.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The integer IDs are an encoding; a lookup table translates them back, e.g. 17 → cat, 15 → bench, 2 → bicycle in listing 12.3.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Needed whenever we display ground truth or predictions with readable labels.

terminology.meaning: Keras library of pretrained models and utilities, imported as `keras_hub` in listing 12.1.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s visualize an example image to make this a little more concrete. We
paragraphs.what_it_says: To make things concrete, the authors define a Matplotlib function to draw an image and another to draw a labelled box, both used throughout the chapter. Each new label gets a new colour via the HSV colour space: saturation and brightness are fixed and only the hue changes, producing bright colours that stand out.
paragraphs.what_it_means: HSV separates 'which colour' (hue) from 'how vivid' (saturation) and 'how bright' (value). Varying only hue keeps every box equally vivid and readable while changing its colour.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Clear visualization is how you will judge, by eye, whether targets and predictions make sense (figures 12.3–12.9).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Stepping the hue by 0.618 (the golden-ratio conjugate) mod 1 spreads successive hues nearly evenly around the colour wheel without knowing in advance how many labels there will be — consecutive labels are never assigned similar colours.

terminology.meaning: Hue, saturation, value: an alternative to RGB where hue is the position on the colour wheel.
The 'colour' itself as an angle on the colour wheel, expressed in [0, 1) by Matplotlib.

connections: p.359: the rest of the helpers and figure 12.3, the sample image drawn with them

concepts.name: COCO dataset statistics
concepts.definition: The parsed training set: 117,266 images, 1–63 boxes per image, integer labels below 91.
concepts.intuition: Lots of images, very variable numbers of objects per image.
concepts.technical: Each record has normalized `boxes`, integer `labels` and a `path`; names come from `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name`.
concepts.significance: Defines the shape of the learning problem the YOLO model must solve.
concepts.misconception: That 91 distinct classes appear — 91 is the ID range size; COCO 2017 detection uses 80 classes.

concepts.name: Golden-ratio hue generation
concepts.definition: Assigning the k-th label the hue (0.618·k) mod 1 at fixed saturation and value.
concepts.intuition: Each step jumps ~222° around the colour wheel, so successive colours are far apart and the wheel fills evenly.
concepts.technical: Implemented in `label_to_color` with `s = 0.5`, `v = 0.9` and `hsv_to_rgb`; label 0 is reserved as gray.
concepts.significance: Unlimited distinct, bright label colours with no predefined palette.
concepts.example: Hues 0.618, 0.236, 0.854, 0.472, 0.090 for the first five new labels.
concepts.misconception: That the colour depends on the label ID — it depends on the order in which labels are first seen.

concepts.name: Drawing a bounding box
concepts.definition: Rendering an `[x, y, w, h]` box as an outline rectangle on an image.
concepts.intuition: Corner plus size is exactly what Matplotlib's `Rectangle` takes.
concepts.technical: `Rectangle((x, y), w, h, lw=2, ec=color, fc="none")` on axes whose limits are the unit square (set in `draw_image`, p.359).
concepts.significance: Lets normalized boxes be drawn directly, without converting to pixels.
concepts.example: Box [0.12, 0.27, 0.57, 0.33] (the cat) drawn from (0.12, 0.27) with width 0.57 and height 0.33.
concepts.misconception: That the boxes must be converted back to pixels before drawing — the axes themselves are set to [0, 1].

math.title: Hue of the k-th new label

variables.meaning: `len(color_map)` when the label is first seen: 1 for the first new label, since 0 is pre-filled with gray.
Hue in [0, 1) (fraction of the colour wheel).

math.operations: Multiply by 0.618, keep the fractional part.
math.purpose: Generate well-separated hues for an unknown number of labels.
math.interpretation: Because 0.618 is (close to) irrational, the sequence never repeats and fills [0, 1) nearly uniformly; each new hue falls in the largest remaining gap.
math.intuition: Like placing seeds in a sunflower: the golden angle avoids clustering.
math.numerical_example: k = 1..5: 0.618, 0.236, 0.854, 0.472, 0.090 — blue, yellow-green, pink, cyan, orange.

code.title: Visualizing a COCO image with box annotations (first part)
code.what_it_does: Defines a cached label→colour mapping using golden-ratio hue steps, and starts `draw_box`, which draws an unfilled rectangle for a normalized box. The listing continues on p.359 with the label text box and `draw_image`.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports: pyplot for figures, `hsv_to_rgb` to convert HSV to RGB, `Rectangle` patch for boxes.
Global cache; label 0 is pre-assigned gray (inference: likely for 'no object'/background cells in later visualizations).

For an unseen label, hue = `(len(color_map) * 0.618) % 1` with saturation 0.5 and value 0.9 (callout: 'Uses the golden ratio to generate new hues of a bright color with the HSV colorspace'); convert and cache it. Seen labels return their cached colour.
`draw_box`: unpack the box and add a `Rectangle` anchored at the top-left `(x, y)` with width `w`, height `h`, line width 2, edge colour `color`, no fill. Continues on p.359.

code.inputs_outputs: `label_to_color(label)` → RGB array or 'gray'. `draw_box(ax, box, text, color)` → draws on `ax` (the `text` argument is used in the part on p.359).
code.algorithm: Memoized colour assignment; geometric drawing on unit-square axes.
code.theory_link: Visual inspection of ground truth and predictions.

parameters.name: s = 0.5, v = 0.9
parameters.role: Fixed saturation and brightness for all label colours.

parameters.name: fc="none"
parameters.role: Transparent fill so the image remains visible.

pitfalls: Colours depend on the order labels are first drawn, so the same class can get different colours across sessions.
`Rectangle((x, y), ...)` draws downward from (x, y) only because `draw_image` inverts the y axis (`ylim=(1, 0)`, p.359).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: preview the first hues label_to_color will produce
for k in range(1, 6):
    print(k, round((k * 0.618) % 1, 3))
# 1 0.618, 2 0.236, 3 0.854, 4 0.472, 5 0.09

deeper.title: Why the golden ratio spreads colours well
deeper.body: Successive hues $0.618, 0.236, 0.854, 0.472, 0.090, 0.708, 0.326, 0.944$ (computed, not printed in the book). After 3 colours the gaps around the wheel are about 0.24–0.38; after 5 they are 0.09–0.15. Each new hue lands in one of the largest gaps — a property of the golden ratio (three-distance theorem). A naive step like 0.1 would give 10 colours before repeating and make neighbours look alike; a step of 0.5 would alternate between just two hues.

deeper.title: Reading metadata[435] against figure 12.3
deeper.body:
- Cat (17): `[0.12, 0.27, 0.57, 0.33]` — starts 12% from the left, 27% from the top, spans 57% × 33% of the square.
- Bench (15): `[0.0, 0.15, 0.79, 0.69]` — touches the left edge.
- Bicycle (2): `[0.0, 0.12, 1.0, 0.75]` — the full width.

The heights stop above 1: since $y + h \le 0.87$, the boxes stay inside the vertical band occupied by a landscape image padded to a square (p.357). Compare with the drawing on p.359.

takeaways: The parsed COCO training set has 117,266 images with 1 to 63 boxes each; label IDs go up to 90 (hence 91 slots).
`keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name` decodes label IDs (17 → cat, 15 → bench, 2 → bicycle).
`label_to_color` steps the hue by the golden ratio at fixed saturation and value to make distinct bright colours.
`draw_box` draws normalized `[x, y, w, h]` boxes directly as Matplotlib rectangles.

questions.question: From listing 12.3, how many images does `metadata` contain, and what is the range of boxes per image?
questions.explanation: Printed by `len(metadata)` and the min/max list comprehensions.

questions.question: What hues does `label_to_color` assign to the first three new labels it sees?
questions.answer: len(color_map) is 1, 2, 3 (gray occupies key 0), so hues are 0.618, 0.236 (1.236 mod 1) and 0.854 (1.854 mod 1).
questions.explanation: Apply h = (k·0.618) mod 1 with k = len(color_map).

questions.question: Why does the code vary only the hue in HSV space?
options: Because RGB cannot represent bright colours
To keep all colours equally bright and vivid while making them distinct
To encode the label ID numerically in the colour
questions.answer: To keep all colours equally bright and vivid while making them distinct
questions.explanation: The page: fixing saturation and brightness and updating only the hue produces bright new colours that stand out. RGB can represent them; Matplotlib accepts RGB (hence `hsv_to_rgb`); the colour doesn't encode the ID.

questions.question: What does `max(max(x["labels"]) for x in metadata) + 1` actually measure, and why might it differ from the number of classes?
questions.answer: The size of the integer range 0..max ID. If IDs are non-contiguous (as in COCO, 80 classes with IDs up to 90), the range is larger than the number of distinct classes.
questions.explanation: See the review flag; the expression counts slots, not distinct labels.

questions.question: In `metadata[435]`, which box spans the entire width of the unit square?
questions.explanation: Its box is [0.0, 0.12, 1.0, 0.75] — x = 0, w = 1.0. The cat box has w = 0.57 and the bench box w = 0.79.

questions.question: Which Matplotlib object does `draw_box` add, and with which arguments?
questions.answer: A `Rectangle` patch at `(x, y)` with width `w`, height `h`, `lw=2`, `ec=color`, `fc="none"`, added via `ax.add_patch`.
questions.explanation: From the last line of listing 12.4 on this page.

questions.question: Could you explain why stepping hues by 0.618 is better than stepping by 0.1 or 0.5?
questions.answer: 0.5 alternates between two hues; 0.1 repeats after 10 and gives neighbours similar colours; 0.618 never repeats and keeps successive colours far apart.
questions.explanation: See the 'deeper' note on the golden ratio.
